$comment: The member realm, kept as code. `npm run cli -- configure` creates the realm from `realm` when it is absent and reconciles `realm` and `clients` onto it when it is present; it builds `browserFlow` through the admin API and binds it as the realm's browser flow. The flow is not part of the import payload: a realm import that carries authenticationFlows skips Keycloak's built-in flows and then also needs every authenticator config, which is what made the spike's realm file brittle.

${NAME} placeholders are filled from the environment of the configure run, with the defaults in `values`. Every default is a TEST-ONLY value: the game audience, the token lifetimes (D9 is open), the brute-force numbers (D3 is open) and the CLI redirect. A production deployment supplies its own values and is a separate approval.

Clients: game-cli (public, PKCE, the only client whose tokens carry the game audience), adventures (confidential, PKCE, its own audience and never the game one; its secret is generated by Keycloak, is never in this file, and is read through the admin API by whoever deploys the site) and identity-recorder (a service account holding exactly serviceAccountRoles, which configure grants and scopes and check compares with the account's effective roles).

Signing keys: one ecdsa-generated P-256 provider and nothing that publishes another algorithm (the edge pins ES256). Keys are created with the realm and never replaced by configure; rotation is its own procedure. `check` fails when the published key set is anything other than ES256 EC keys.

Required actions: `requiredActions` is the complete set that is enabled, not a minimum. A signed-in member can start any enabled action through kc_action, and Keycloak enables UPDATE_PASSWORD, CONFIGURE_TOTP, UPDATE_PROFILE and others by default (UPDATE_PASSWORD gives a passkey member a password credential). configure disables every action not listed and `check` fails on any that is enabled. The three listed are adding a passkey, (re)generating recovery codes and deleting a credential.

userProfile.$comment: A member account holds a username and nothing else a member can see or edit: no name, no email (no email claim reaches any token). Keycloak will not delete the email attribute, so it stays, optional and admin-only. check fails on any other attribute, on any required attribute but username, and on an unmanaged-attribute policy.

events.$comment: Keycloak stores these events so the identity-restore recorder (workloads/identity-restore) can copy them off-host. The list is the complete set, compared exactly by check: the recorder's own required types, plus the error, token and logout types an investigation needs. Admin events are stored with their representations. The 30-day expiries are TEST-ONLY: how long security events are kept is not decided. The admin-event expiry is not part of /events/config; it is the realm attribute adminEventsExpiration, in seconds.

browserFlow.description: Username, then a passkey or a recovery code (fixA). A username with no usable credential is refused; no set-up page is reachable before authentication.

clients.name: Identity recorder
clients.description: Service account the identity-restore recorder signs in as. It reads events and the realm's settings and nothing else. Keycloak generates its secret.
